strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring social-stereotype preferences in masked language models and tracking changes after continued training. Evaluating predictions under the models’ masked-token objective is well motivated.

The experiments cover four standard models, including distilled variants, and two established benchmarks. Extensive category-level results reveal meaningful variation across models, metrics, and datasets.

The token-level examples make the proposed prediction-quality scores interpretable. Retraining on stereotypical and anti-stereotypical sentences generally produces the expected directional changes, providing preliminary evidence that the measures can serve as training diagnostics.
weaknesses: The retraining experiment does not adequately separate bias measurement from memorization. Section 4.3 describes an 80/20 training/validation split, but reports bias evaluation across CPS without identifying an independent test set. The reported 100% accuracy concerns 72 aggregate model/category/direction cases whose labels are assumed from the training condition. This demonstrates sensitivity to the intervention, but does not establish accurate measurement of social bias. Evaluation on held-out pairs and neutral or balanced retraining controls is needed.

The human-agreement evidence is weak. Figure 3 shows best proposed AUCs of 0.571 versus AUL’s 0.569 for BERT, and 0.572 versus 0.566 for RoBERTa. These small improvements lack confidence intervals or paired significance tests, with only 58 negative pairs. Moreover, annotations identify whether the text expresses a stereotype; they do not directly validate the magnitude or direction of a particular model’s bias. The construction of pair-level prediction scores and the statement about selecting thresholds to maximize AUC also require clarification.

Several substantive conclusions exceed the evidence. Calling other metrics’ results ‘underestimates’ or ‘overestimates’ of religious or disability bias treats the proposed measures as a reference standard without independent validation. Differences between metrics establish disagreement, not which estimate is correct. Prediction quality can also reflect lexical frequency, tokenization, and sentence plausibility; the experiments do not sufficiently distinguish these influences from social bias.

The statistical analyses do not consistently test the claims being made. Welch’s tests ignore the matched sentence-pair design, and significance within one model but not another does not establish a difference between models. McNemar’s test assesses changes in binary preference outcomes, whereas Equation 16 counts increases in continuous preference differences; these are different estimands. More frequent significance therefore does not establish greater measurement accuracy. Paired analyses, direct model comparisons, and uncertainty estimates are needed.

The contribution of the metric modifications is insufficiently isolated. Equation 10 changes CRR from 1 − 1/rank to an attention-weighted 1 + log(rank), simultaneously changing the rank transformation and adding attention. It consequently remains nonzero for a perfectly predicted token, unlike CRR and the probability-gap measures. This needs justification and separate ablations. An ordinary all-token masked pseudo-log-likelihood baseline would also help establish the value of the proposed transformations.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript names checkpoints and reports epochs, masking probability, and hardware, but omits learning rate, optimizer, batch size, random seeds, exact splits, and precise attention aggregation details. No implementation link is provided. Equations 1–2 also sum over all sentence tokens despite describing baselines operating on different token subsets. These implementation ambiguities and the unresolved validation concerns prevent a sound Findings recommendation; the approach appears viable for revision and resubmission next cycle.
